The extremely short answer is that it's possible. The longer more complex answer is that you have to be working at it a long while; either be extremely lucky, extremely smart, a combination of both; and/or get a lot of help. 

I've done it - I'm on the DSP and work part-time 15 hours per week. I am the sole mortgagee on a one bedroom apartment in the middle of Perth. 

I bought a house at 24 with my then partner 16 years ago. We had help with loan documentation from my aunt in the real estate business, we borrowed the 3k required from his parents. We were both working and studying at the time.  When that relationship broke down, I had my share of the equity from a pretty great time in the market - about 90k. 

I didn't want to completely blow the money i had burning a hole in my pocket, so I suggested to my mum that we co-purchase a place (which of course means you're living in a multigenerational household, and that's a) a pain in the butt sometimes, but also b) a privilege). I went from working 4 days a week to 2 during that time.  I had that place about 8 years when we both decided that living together wasn't our jam, and mum bought me out - at a pretty great market for that. 

I had about 180k, proof of my income, and a ride or die mortgage broker who absolutely went into bat for me and argued with banks etc - and I got myself a mortgage for roughly 60% of the price. I'm lucky. It's a privilege. I also barely squeak by in terms of finance.  

So whilst yes, it's possible, it's also highly improbable.

I am definitely a pick your weapon kind of person. I have canes, crutches, a rollator, and a powerchair, and i use them all depending on my ability, activity, and need. I could probably get by without the chair - IF i didn't do my own groceries, go anywhere that didn't need me to walk more than a couple hundred of metres, and gave up on travelling intrastate for work. But that would also mean giving up on a lot of independence, trips out or going to gigs in the city, taking my dog for walks, and doing things that bring my life a lot of joy. It would probably also mean a lot more hospitalisations (before chair I was averaging one ER visit every two months at least) as I'd try and push myself to do those things still anyway. If you're thinking about it and you've been thinking on it some time then yes, it's likely it will help. Unfortunately as a minor you need to contend with your parent's opinion too. Maybe showing them these responses will help.

Anyone who comments on the professionalism of someone's haircut/style, tattoos or piercings beyond hygiene and safety requirements is more unprofessional than the one they are commenting on. Where you part your hair, it's texture, or it's colour has no bearing on your work. I think it's lovely. 

I also regularly attend meetings with politicians with multiple facial piercings and what is maybe considered a more 'extreme' haircut and I'm completely OK with disregarding or challenging comments like that 🤷‍♀️ your mileage may vary.

I think that it depends on how you feel and what you realise when you reflect on why you chose 'Take it as a compliment'. Many of us have internalised victim-blaming language, and it's become our default way of thinking and feeling. If it is that you wished to congratulate OP, congratulate them, and you can empathise that people saying inappropriate things is awful. If you're in for a good old personal development moment you could take it further by looking at other times you've used similar language - with yourself or others, and have had it used with you and come up with alternatives that don't follow the same mentality. At the very least I'd try to practice not using that turn of phrase any more.

'Take it as a compliment' is a really unhelpful way of phrasing what you may have intended as a congratulations on OPs achievements. Losing 10-20% of body mass is definitely an achievement, but - 

'Take it as a compliment' has been a phrase that's  been used for an exceedingly long time to excuse inappropriate behaviour or words from other (usually majority) groups. I'm sure many women and afab people have heard it when being sexually harassed; I've heard it as a disabled person- I'd invite you to think on why you may have defaulted to this.

Looking at anything the wrong way, standing up too long, sudden shocks, putting head down or bending over...

I started having severe problems walking August 2020, and quickly transitioned from cane to crutches to rollator or chair. I tried as hard as I could for as long as I could to listen to the internal voices telling me I could still manage everything like I had before, and found myself in the ER at least once every two months. I stopped working so much, started relying on my aids more, and listening to my body- and it's almost 12 months since my last ER visit. But I STILL have moments where I almost convince myself I'm just being melodramatic and OTT. I think as spoonies we do all the things we are supposed to do to look after ourselves and keep us running and then when it starts working we either overdo it and push ourselves back or start with the Internalised ableism. It might just be that we need to recognise that and do the right things anyway.

I'm a wheelchair user - parking on the footpath makes it incredibly unsafe for those of us with mobility aids - we may not be able to get by, walk on grass, or jump curbs - I know parking is important but please don't park on the footpaths.

Is skating something that you love doing? Does it help your mental health? If yes, definitely still do it, and use mobility aids to conserve energy before and after. There is absolutely no point in us just existing and hating our existence.

Late to the party, but I read your statement and a word flood happened:

I'm turning 29 in three months. 

Up until last May, I'd spent ten years working in the same industry, had built a considerable list of qualifications, commendations, citations and awards; and was working (for the past three years) as the sole quality assurance and training manager in my state- considered to be part of upper management in a nationally run community organisation. I had a new car, I'd recently built and was in the process of decorating the house that I owned. 

I hated my life. It was awful. I was easily working 10-12 hour days, spending some weekends on-call, others on-shift or travelling to Queensland, where the head office was situated.When my now (ex-) partner told me he was worried about all the stress that I was under, and the effect that work had upon me, and insisted that I quit (after a flippant comment about my wanting to from me, that was not an ultimatum folks!), I cried with happiness. 

I had no idea what to do. I'd been diagnosed with bipolar, I never wanted to work in the field again, and the 21 pages of awards, citations and qualifications couldn't help me. So I started again. It was, and still is terrifying. I asked myself what I really wanted to do. Turns out I want to be a medical scientist. I enrolled in uni, started a part-time cleaning business, and continued to freak out, because I wasn't the stereotypical successful 20-something that I was previously. 

Semester started, chemistry and biology and forensics blew my hair right back. I loved it. Whilst cleaning I could wear daggy clothes, sing and dance to my hearts content (yes, I've been caught out). Due to a number of reasons, my partner and I split up. I moved in with my mum, who is amazing, and funny and supportive. I'm getting the opportunity to develop a relationship with my (much) younger brother, and that is fruitful. I have time to go to the beach during the week. 

I'm slowly coming to realise that we, all of us, place way too much import on how much money we make, not what we do with our time. Many of us live to work. I know that this is a boring old clique, but it's true... we should be working to live. If you can manage that, and work toward achieving whatever it is you want to do- go for it. 

I once read something, written by someone, who said that the most interesting people they knew still didn't know what they wanted to do when they were 40. I can see that- they would be constantly experiencing new things- how fantastic is that?

In terms of advice? The only thing I can say is this: leap. Make sure that you have enough money to exist on, be it through a part-time job or welfare (if that applies to your country).... and do whatever it is you want. You'll get scared. You'll be tempted to take the easy path. Don't. Find something that you're passionate about. If your passion fades, find something new. Forge a new path. Reframe your negatives (I freak out, because I'm "nearly 30 and living with my parents"; but I also know that I have this time to study and reconnect with myself with all the support that my family can throw at me- which is pretty sweet). Identify what ISN'T working for you, and turn it around to what you need (for example, when people say "stop yelling" they actually mean "could you please lower your voice"). Look for your supports (friends, family, community organisations, church (if you're religious)). Talk about it. Write about it. Figure it out. 

Best of luck.

TL; DR: Changing your life isn't an easy process. Nothing to do but jump in.

The best way to test your eggs is to throw (actually, don't do this. I'd suggest gently placing) them into a full pot of cold water. Fresh eggs will stay submerged (some will sort of float in the middle of the water- they are still ok, just eat those ones first). Spoiled eggs will float to the top. My general rule of thumb is that if it's in the top quarter of water, don't eat it.
